sections.title: Finite branching makes an infinite path

passages.title: The hypothesis is local finiteness
passages.text: A rooted tree is connected and has a unique finite route from every vertex to its root. Here each vertex has finitely many children, but there need not be one common bound on their number. The theorem says: if this tree has infinitely many vertices, it contains a sequence v₀,v₁,… beginning at the root, with vⱼ₊₁ a child of vⱼ for every nonnegative integer j. Our downward arrows follow children; the source’s oriented-tree arrows point toward the parent. The existence claim is the same. The vertical bars count members of the children set, and ∞ means unbounded size; the condition says every individual node has only finitely many immediate children.

passages.title: Choose a subtree that cannot run out
passages.text: The root has infinitely many descendants. If every one of its finitely many child subtrees were finite, their finite union together with the root would be finite, a contradiction. At least one child therefore has infinitely many descendants. Repeat this argument at the selected child. Induction supplies a next vertex at every finite stage, and the nested choices form the infinite path. This argument, rather than a large animation, proves the theorem.
passages.formula: \text{finite union of finite sets is finite}

passages.title: Watch a defined infinite spine
passages.text: The model defines pⱼ to have children pⱼ₊₁ and fⱼ, with fⱼ terminal, for every j≥0. Only a finite window is displayed. The rule defining the family establishes continuation beyond the window; merely drawing a long chain would not. To recognize a child with infinitely many descendants can require information unavailable to an algorithm, so the existence proof is not a general effective path-finding procedure.

passages.title: Why infinitely many children changes everything
passages.text: Let one root have a separate finite chain of length m for every positive integer m. This tree has arbitrarily large finite depth and infinitely many vertices, but every root-starting path chooses one chain and then ends. Its root has infinitely many children, violating the hypothesis. With finite branching, each finite level is finite; consequently an infinite tree must have unbounded depth. Without finite branching that reasoning and the theorem both fail.
passages.formula: \forall m\ \exists\text{ a path of length }m\ \not\Rightarrow\ \exists\text{ infinite path}

sections.title: Count ordered and binary tree shapes

passages.title: State exactly what a shape remembers
passages.text: A binary shape is empty or is a root with two distinguished child positions, left and right. Vertices carry no labels, but swapping unequal children changes the shape. Let Cₙ count shapes with n internal vertices, including the empty shape C₀=1. An ordered general tree instead has a finite ordered list of children. These families have related counts, not identical size parameters.

passages.title: Split the size at the root
passages.text: For n≥1, the left child has some i vertices with 0≤i<n; the right has n−1−i. Choosing one shape on each side gives CᵢCₙ₋₁₋ᵢ possibilities. Different splits cannot coincide because the left size is recoverable, and different pairs cannot coincide because both child shapes are recoverable. This disjoint decomposition proves the recurrence, including the empty-child cases.

passages.title: Turn pair construction into a series
passages.text: Write C(z)=Σₙ≥₀Cₙzⁿ as a formal power series. Multiplication records all ordered pairs, and the extra root contributes z, giving C=1+zC². The solution with constant coefficient 1 is (1−√(1−4z))/(2z), interpreted by its removable formal constant term. Coefficient extraction gives Cₙ=(2n choose n)/(n+1). Our grid enumerates all root splits for n=4 and sums 5+2+2+5=14.

passages.title: The one-vertex size shift matters
passages.text: Removing the root of an ordered tree leaves an ordered forest. The first-child/next-sibling encoding maps that forest bijectively to a binary tree on the same remaining vertices. Thus ordered general trees on m≥1 vertices are counted by Cₘ₋₁. Forgetting child order is not this bijection: it identifies shapes under symmetry and leads to different counts. A lone ordered root corresponds to the empty binary shape, not the one-node binary shape.

title: Count unlabeled rooted and free trees

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Explain multisets of child shapes and symmetry; use centroid/rooting correction. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

sections.title: Count unlabeled rooted and free trees

passages.title: Unordered children form a multiset
passages.text: Let aₙ count rooted unlabeled trees with n≥1 vertices, where children have no left-to-right order, and put a₀=0. The children are a multiset of rooted shapes. Each particular k-vertex shape may occur zero, one, two, or more times, contributing 1/(1−zᵏ). Since there are aₖ such shapes, multiply these factors and then attach one root. The identity is formal: any fixed coefficient depends on only finitely many factors. Write A(z)=Σ_{n≥1} a_n z^n: the coefficient of z^n counts rooted shapes of size n. The variable z records size; it is not a vertex label.

passages.title: Compute coefficients without guessing symmetry factors
passages.text: Taking the formal logarithmic derivative of A(z)/z gives zA′/A−1=Σₖ≥₁bₖzᵏ, where bₖ=Σd|k d a_d. Matching coefficients yields (n−1)aₙ=Σₖ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹ bₖaₙ₋ₖ. This recurrence produces 1,1,2,4,9,20 for sizes one through six. Independently, the model decodes all small labeled trees, erases labels via sorted parenthesis codes, and checks the resulting distinct rooted isomorphism classes. The condition d|k means d is a positive divisor of k. Thus b_4=1·a_1+2·a_2+4·a_4; the prime on A′ denotes formal differentiation of the series.

passages.title: Remove the root using centroids, not division
passages.text: For a vertex v of an n-vertex free tree, remove v and take the largest component size as its weight. A centroid minimizes this weight. There is one centroid, or two adjacent centroids whose connecting edge divides the tree into equal halves. Use this invariant central element: the unique centroid vertex, or the edge joining the two centroids. A tree marked at its central element represents one free shape. Every other vertex-marked tree corresponds to an edge directed toward that center, by taking the first edge from its marked vertex. Every noncentral edge-marked tree corresponds to that edge directed away from the center. These assignments are reversible; when the center is an edge, its two orientations arise from marking its two endpoint vertices. Hence vertex-marked trees plus undirected-edge-marked trees equal free trees plus directed-edge-marked trees. Cutting a directed marked edge gives an ordered pair of rooted trees, counted by A². Cutting an undirected marked edge gives an unordered pair, counted by (A²+A(z²))/2: distinct pairs occur twice in A², while equal pairs need the diagonal correction. Solving A+(A²+A(z²))/2=F+A² yields F=A−A²/2+A(z²)/2. This is a bijective counting argument, not division by the number of possible root positions. F(z)=Σ_{n≥1} f_n z^n records free, unrooted shapes, while A(z) records rooted shapes. Products of these series count pairs whose vertex counts add.

passages.title: Check a symmetry counterexample
passages.text: A four-vertex path gives only two rooted shapes: root at an endpoint or at an interior vertex. A four-vertex star also gives two: root at the center or at a leaf. Together these are the four rooted shapes but only two free shapes. Dividing four by four would give one, which is wrong. Canonicalization uses structure alone; vertex names, drawing positions, and edge orientations introduced only for display must not alter the class. Here f_n counts free shapes of size n. The bracket [2|n] is 1 when n is even and 0 otherwise; it enables the equal-half correction only when two halves of size n/2 are possible.

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

passages.title: Two related codes have different lengths
passages.text: For a labeled undirected tree on {1,…,n}, n≥2, the standard Prüfer word has length n−2. Repeatedly remove the smallest labeled leaf and output its sole neighbor, stopping with two vertices. The source also gives a rooted canonical code: retain the designated root, remove the smallest other leaf, and continue until only that root remains, producing n−1 symbols. We implement both and distinguish their domains.

passages.title: Recover the next leaf from the remaining word
passages.text: In a Prüfer word, the current degree of a remaining vertex equals one plus its occurrences in the remaining suffix. Hence the smallest vertex absent from that suffix is the next leaf. Join it to the first symbol, delete it from availability, and remove that symbol. At the end join the last two vertices. Each added edge removes a leaf from consideration, so decoding cannot create a cycle and yields a connected tree.

passages.title: Count words only after proving bijection
passages.text: There are n choices in each of n−2 Prüfer positions, so nⁿ⁻² labeled free trees for n≥2. Designating an arbitrary root multiplies by n; fixing one root does not. The rooted n−1 code correspondingly has nⁿ⁻¹ possibilities. For n=2 the Prüfer word is empty and describes the one edge. For n=1 the single-vertex tree is handled separately; a negative word length is not meaningful.

title: Internal and external path lengths

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Extend binary trees with external nodes; derive E=I+2n and extremal shapes. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

passages.title: A null child is a measurable position
passages.text: Extend a binary tree by placing an external square at every empty child position. Original vertices are internal circles. Every internal vertex has exactly two children in the extended tree; every external vertex has none. If there are n internal and s external vertices, edge counting gives 2n=n+s−1, hence s=n+1. This includes the empty original tree: one external root at depth zero. Here n counts circles and s counts external squares; it does not count the depth labels printed inside them.

passages.title: Separate the two sums
passages.text: Depth counts edges from the root, so the root has depth zero. Internal path length I is the sum of depths over circles; external path length E is the corresponding sum over squares. Neither is height, which is a maximum rather than a sum. Null positions matter because an unsuccessful descent can reach them even though they are not stored data records. The notation d(v) means the depth of vertex v. Each sum adds one such depth for every vertex of its specified kind.

passages.title: One expansion proves the identity
passages.text: Replace an external vertex at depth d by an internal vertex with two external children. Internal path length rises by d. External path length replaces d by 2(d+1), rising by d+2. The computed sequence confirms concrete cases but does not replace this induction.

sections.title: Balance depth without changing node count

passages.title: A depth budget has limited shallow slots
passages.text: In a binary tree at most 2ᵈ vertices can occupy depth d. To minimize a sum of n depths, fill the smallest available depths first. A complete tree realizes that capacity pattern, so the lower bound is attainable. Number its internal vertices in breadth-first order from 1 to n; vertex k has depth floor(log₂k). Completeness is sufficient, but when the last level is partial the minimizing shape need not be unique.

passages.title: Move depth without changing the count
passages.text: The scene contrasts a five-vertex chain with a five-vertex complete tree. Both contain five data vertices, yet their depth sums are 10 and 6. A chain maximizes the sum: depth of the jth vertex in any ancestor-first listing is at most j−1, so I≤0+1+⋯+(n−1). Equality is achieved when all vertices lie on one path. External path extrema follow immediately from E=I+2n.

passages.title: Evaluate the minimum exactly
passages.text: For n≥0 let q=floor(log₂(n+1)); then summing the complete levels yields Imin=(n+1)q−2^(q+1)+2. Our implementation uses integer bit lengths, avoiding floating-point errors at powers of two. The empty case n=0 gives zero. This result minimizes an unweighted depth sum; it is not the answer when some leaves are much more likely or costly than others.

passages.title: Generalize the capacity argument
passages.text: For t≥2, depth d holds at most tᵈ internal vertices. Fill levels until n places are occupied; the remaining vertices occupy the next depth. With q=floor(log_t((t−1)n+1)), the exact minimum is (n+1/(t−1))q−(t^(q+1)−t)/(t−1)². In one-based breadth-first numbering, parent(k)=floor((k+t−2)/t) for k≥2. The model verifies the formula with exact rational arithmetic against explicit parent chains.

passages.title: Weights change what balance should mean
passages.text: Given m positive leaf weights wᵢ, minimize W=Σwᵢℓᵢ over full binary trees whose leaves carry those weights, with ℓᵢ their depths. Leaf order is unrestricted. Larger weights should tend to be shallower, so minimizing height or making every depth similar is not necessarily optimal. If an application requires alphabetic leaf order, this unrestricted Huffman problem is a different optimization problem.

check.prompt: Can a required left-to-right leaf order invalidate a Huffman exchange?

passages.title: Why the two smallest can be siblings
passages.text: Take an optimal tree and a deepest sibling pair of leaves. If a smaller weight occupies a shallower position than a larger weight, exchanging them changes cost by (small−large)(deep−shallow)≤0. Repeated exchanges place the two smallest weights at that deepest pair without increasing the optimum. This exchange argument establishes the greedy choice; sorting once and pairing adjacent original weights would not establish it.

passages.title: Contract the chosen pair
passages.text: If sibling leaves have weights a,b, replace their parent subtree by a leaf of weight a+b. Expanding it later adds one depth to exactly those weights, adding cost a+b. An optimal solution containing that pair must contract to an optimal smaller solution, or substitution would improve it. Induction therefore justifies repeatedly merging the two currently smallest available weights, including previously merged subtrees. The example uses weights 3,4,8,10.

passages.title: Verify cost and handle ties honestly
passages.text: The sum of all merge weights equals weighted path length because every merge counts once for each leaf below it. Our independent oracle explores every possible merge pair at every stage for small positive inputs and compares the minimum with the greedy result. Ties can produce distinct optimal trees; deterministic tie-breaking makes the display reproducible, not uniquely optimal. For one leaf the cost is zero under the empty-code convention.

title: Sharing defeats naive deletion

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Maintain reference counts and explain cyclic garbage; distinguish roots from internal references. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

passages.title: Ownership is not the same as one incoming edge
passages.text: Shared structures allow several root variables or heap fields to refer to the same object. Deleting a single reference does not authorize deleting that object while another live reference remains. A reference count must include every counted root slot and heap link, and every update must adjust counts consistently. Object identity is independent of the value stored inside it. The abbreviation rc(v) is the reference count of object v; the # sign means count the listed incoming references, including repeated references from different fields.

passages.title: A zero count permits cascading reclamation
passages.text: When a count becomes zero, reclaim that object and decrement the counts of its outgoing targets. Those targets may then become zero, forming a cascade. The model recomputes counts and performs this exact cascade. The root A reaches a diamond-shaped shared object D; D is not freed merely because one branch stops referring to it. This argument assumes the count is exact and there are no hidden uncounted references.

passages.title: A positive count does not prove liveness
passages.text: The disconnected pair X→Y→X has positive counts even with no root path to either object. After removing the last root of the ordinary component, reference counting can reclaim that component but leaves the cyclic garbage. In the scene red objects are actually reclaimed; surviving unmarked cyclic objects are still allocated, despite being unreachable. A one-object self-loop is already a counterexample.

passages.title: Choose the semantic contract before the collector
passages.text: Reachability-based liveness is the existence of a path from a complete set of roots through recognized pointer fields. Counts approximate that property operationally but do not characterize it in cyclic graphs. Conversely, omitting an actual root can make any collector unsafe. Counter overflow, weak references, concurrent updates, and finalizers require additional rules beyond this stop-the-world finite-graph model.

passages.title: Find liveness before changing allocation
passages.text: Take a finite allocated-object set V, a complete root set, and a pointer graph whose edges target allocated objects or null. Pause mutation during this teaching collector. Start with all mark bits clear. Marking answers which objects are reachable; sweeping answers which allocated objects may become free. Mixing these phases prematurely risks reclaiming a reachable object whose path has not yet been explored. R denotes the objects reachable from roots, G the garbage objects, and V all currently allocated objects. The set difference V\R means the allocated objects not in R.

passages.title: Mark before putting work on the frontier
passages.text: Mark each root and put newly marked objects on a work stack. Pop an object, inspect each of its pointer fields, and mark and schedule each previously unmarked target. Marking before scheduling prevents duplicate work on shared targets and prevents an infinite loop on cycles. Every discovered object is reachable, since it is a root or follows a pointer from another reachable object.

passages.title: An empty frontier establishes closure
passages.text: When the stack becomes empty, every marked object has had its outgoing fields inspected. Thus the marked set contains the roots and is closed under graph edges. Every finite root path stays in this closed set, so R is contained in marked. Combined with the other inclusion, marked=R. Only then does a sweep through V reclaim unmarked objects. The disconnected X,Y cycle is reclaimed; a rooted cycle would be retained.

passages.title: Count cost and acknowledge roots
passages.text: With adjacency lists, stack marking uses O(|R|+|E_R|) work, and sweeping all allocated slots costs O(|V|). Mark storage costs one bit per object plus a possibly large frontier. An atom has no pointer fields to traverse, even if its payload resembles an address. Real implementations must describe root registers, stacks, globals and valid object layouts accurately; our diagram cannot discover references omitted from its input. E_R is the set of outgoing pointer edges from reachable objects. The bars |V| and |E_R| count objects and edges respectively; T is total work.

passages.title: The collector also needs memory
passages.text: An ordinary DFS or marking worklist may need many pending pointers precisely when free storage is exhausted. The frontier must come from a reserved budget, a safe reusable field, or a strategy that repeats work. Simply dropping entries from a full stack is incorrect: some marked objects would never have their outgoing edges examined. H is the maximum number of pending object pointers the frontier can hold; |frontier| counts the pointers currently stored there.

passages.title: A bounded frontier requires remembered obligations
passages.text: Our explicit teaching variant uses capacity H≥1, a mark bit, and a separate processed bit per object. Newly discovered objects are marked even if the frontier is full. When the frontier empties, scan for marked-but-unprocessed objects and refill it. Every reachable object is eventually processed because processing grows monotonically and scans recover every unsatisfied obligation. This variant is not a literal implementation of the source’s Algorithm C and openly pays for an extra bit.

passages.title: Alternative representations make different promises
passages.text: The source’s bounded-stack rescanning scheme tracks a safe restart position rather than our full processed-bit set. Header-field stacks can avoid a separate pointer array, but only if those fields are genuinely available and the list structure is well formed at every collection point. Interior roots and temporary malformed lists can violate that assumption. Lower auxiliary space may trade for rescanning time; no universal optimal H follows from this small demonstration.

title: Reverse pointers and restore them

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Trace Schorr-Waite-style marking; encode return paths in existing links without losing the graph. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

passages.title: A return path can live in borrowed fields
passages.text: This is the source’s two-link pointer-reversal marking algorithm, expressed with fields A, B, MARK and ATOM. ATOM=1 identifies a payload leaf whose links are ignored. The graph may contain cycles and sharing. Collection is stop-the-world: other code must not read the temporarily altered representation. A few pointer registers P,Q,T replace an external traversal stack; per-node control and mark bits still exist. P is the current object, Q is a saved child pointer, and T is the top of the return chain. A and B are the two link-field names, not the identities of particular nodes.

passages.title: Reverse one edge while retaining its missing target
passages.text: Before descending an unmarked A child, save the child in Q, replace A(P) by T, set the temporary ATOM bit, and move T to P and P to Q. The child that used to occupy the changed field remains recoverable from the current traversal. For a B descent the B field holds the return link and the temporary control bit distinguishes that case. Mark tests prevent following a cycle indefinitely.

passages.title: Restoration is part of correctness
passages.text: On return, T locates the suspended parent. Its control bit tells whether A or B is borrowed. Save the older T from that field before replacing the field with P, then move P back to the parent and restore the bit. An A return proceeds to inspect B; a B return continues upward. The computed trace displays actual temporary field values, not the original graph behind a decorative cursor.

passages.title: Prove preservation, then check every small graph
passages.text: The invariant is that suspended ancestors form a return chain in the borrowed fields, with the missing downward edge represented by the next active object and the phase. Descending extends that encoding; returning exactly reverses the corresponding local update. Marking finishes with precisely the original root-reachable objects marked, P restored to its initial root, and every original field restored. Tests exhaust all three-vertex two-link graphs; finite testing is implementation evidence alongside this invariant, not a proof for all graph sizes.

passages.title: One update may have several local obligations
passages.text: Moving a field to another group changes its containment parent and sibling neighborhood; renaming it changes its name-index membership. Neither action automatically implies the other. A representation invariant should state for each relation which heads own a chain and which reciprocal facts must agree. For example, each child listed under a group must name that group as parent, while every node on a same-name chain must carry that indexed name. The builder reads positive level numbers: an increase opens a child group, an equal level adds a sibling, and a decrease pops to a matching prior level. Nonconsecutive levels are allowed, but a decrease landing between existing levels is rejected as mixed sibling levels.

passages.title: More links are an explicit tradeoff
passages.text: An extra parent link may replace repeated root-to-node searches with immediate access, but consumes space and adds maintenance work. An index can accelerate queries while becoming stale if updates forget it. There is no universal best record format independent of the operations and workload. Our model inspects the table and its structural invariants; it also executes a level-number table builder, but does not claim a full compiler, transactional editor, or concurrent index implementation.

passages.title: A short name starts a candidate set
passages.text: An unqualified field name can occur in multiple groups. Search all nodes with that name, then test any supplied qualifiers. In the source’s hierarchical qualification convention, DAY OF ARRIVAL may omit the intermediate DATE group: each later name need only occur farther up the ancestor chain. The qualifiers must retain their order and must each match a distinct ancestor position. A_0 is the requested field name, followed by ancestor names A_1 through A_k in the written order. For DAY OF ARRIVAL, A_0=DAY and A_1=ARRIVAL; these are names to match, not node IDs.

passages.title: Walk ancestors, not adjacent text
passages.text: For each candidate named A₀, move repeatedly to its parent. Advance to the next requested qualifier only when the current ancestor’s name matches. Reaching the root before consuming all qualifiers rejects that candidate. This is a subsequence test on the ancestor-name chain, not a string substring test or an assumption that all qualifiers are immediate parents. The positive integers d_1,…,d_k count parent steps from candidate v. Parent^{d_j}(v) means follow the parent link d_j times, so the strict inequalities require distinct ancestors in the requested order.

passages.title: Correspondence is structural, not positional
passages.text: Two records can store matching elementary fields in different orders. Pairing the first leaf with the first leaf is therefore unsafe. Define a correspondence key from an item’s name and all ancestor names relative to its record root; this applies to elementary items and groups alike. The source requires complete relative qualification at equal depth here, unlike the abbreviated qualifiers used for a single-name query. A corresponding pair is output as soon as either side is elementary; if both sides are groups, matching descends into equal-name children.

title: Reserve variable-sized blocks

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Implement first fit and best fit; split blocks and expose external fragmentation. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

passages.title: Make every byte belong somewhere
passages.text: Use a finite arena [0,C) partitioned into disjoint half-open blocks [start,start+size). Each block is either free or reserved for one live allocation. A request is for payload bytes, while block size also includes metadata and alignment. In our first model alignment is four bytes and metadata overhead is zero; later boundary-tag examples account for real overhead explicitly. C is the arena’s total byte capacity, r the requested payload bytes, and h the metadata overhead per allocation. The ceiling rounds (r+h)/4 up to a whole number of four-byte units; here h=0, so request 9 needs 4×3=12 bytes.

passages.title: First fit and best fit answer different searches
passages.text: First fit scans the address-ordered free list and stops at the first adequate interval. Best fit scans candidates and chooses the smallest adequate size, breaking ties by address. Both must test the rounded total requirement. A remainder can be split only if it is large enough to form a valid free block; otherwise reserve the entire interval and record the extra internal waste. Search effort is a separate metric from wasted bytes.

passages.title: Freeing is a partition update
passages.text: The caller returns a currently live allocation exactly once. Returning an interior pointer, the wrong size, or an already free block violates this model’s precondition. Marking its interval free preserves all addresses and payloads of other live allocations. The free list is kept sorted by increasing start address so the possible adjacent predecessor and successor can be identified. p is the block’s starting byte address and s its size. The interval [p,p+s) includes p but stops just before p+s, covering exactly s bytes.

passages.title: Adjacency is equality of endpoints
passages.text: Two free intervals can coalesce only when the lower start plus its size equals the upper start. Merely being consecutive entries in the free list does not suffice: a live block may lie between them. After insertion, merge with the next interval when endpoints touch, and then with the preceding interval when endpoints touch. If both neighbors are free, all three become one interval. In p+s=q, p and s are the lower block’s start and size, and q is the next block’s start. For example, [0,8) and [8,16) touch because 0+8=8.

passages.title: Return the bridge last
passages.text: The scene allocates A,B,C, then returns A and C while B remains live. Returning B removes the last live bridge between the neighboring free areas, so they coalesce. The resulting free block spans the full arena. The model checks exact coverage after each operation: no gaps, overlaps, lost bytes or duplicate live IDs can be hidden by the drawing.

passages.title: Coalescing is not compaction
passages.text: Coalescing combines already adjacent free regions and never moves a live byte. Compaction relocates live blocks and requires updating every reference or using stable handles. An address-sorted free list can cost linear search time to find the insertion point; once the neighbors are known, the local merge decisions are constant-size work. A good explanation must separate those costs.

passages.title: Endpoints reveal neighboring blocks
passages.text: A boundary-tag layout stores size and allocation status at block boundaries. For the explicit accounting extension here, reserve a four-byte header and a four-byte footer in every block; an eight-byte payload needs at least sixteen bytes before any extra free-list requirements. The free-list links may use free-block payload space, so the minimum free-block size must accommodate those links too.

passages.title: Read only within validated arena bounds
passages.text: For a block starting at p, its predecessor footer lies immediately before p, unless p is the arena start. A valid footer supplies the predecessor size and status; the successor begins at p+size. Guard the arena ends with allocated sentinels or explicit bounds checks before reading either neighbor. A random previous word is not a valid footer merely because arithmetic produced an address.

passages.title: Unlink neighbors before erasing their metadata
passages.text: There are four cases: neither neighbor free, left only, right only, or both. Remove each free neighbor from the doubly linked free list before combining intervals and rewriting the outside tags. The merged block must appear exactly once in that list, and its header and footer must agree. Our partition scene highlights both ends and demonstrates the two-neighbor case; the executable tests cover all four cases and tag consistency.

passages.title: Local discovery is not free metadata
passages.text: Boundary tags avoid an address-ordered search for adjacent physical blocks, and double links permit removing known free-list entries locally. This does not make an arbitrary allocation search constant time. The main geometry shows whole block sizes; its color strips indicate where endpoint metadata belongs, not an additional uncounted area outside those blocks. The executed model discovers neighbors from guarded tags, unlinks their reciprocal free-list entries, and verifies tag consistency and minimum size. Its Python array sorting and snapshot reconstruction are visualization instrumentation; they are not claimed to be the constant-time linked implementation.
passages.formula: \text{local coalescing work}=O(1)\text{ once block metadata is valid}

title: Split and merge exact buddies

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Implement power-of-two allocation and buddy discovery; distinguish buddies from adjacent blocks. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

passages.title: A binary partition constrains possible intervals
passages.text: Start with an arena of 2ᵐ bytes and represent addresses as offsets from its base. Every block has size 2ᵏ and begins at an offset divisible by 2ᵏ. To satisfy a positive request, round up to a supported power of two, find a free block of at least that order, and repeatedly split it into equal halves. The unused halves go into free sets indexed by order. The exponent m sets the whole arena size; k sets the current block size. x is that block’s offset from the arena base. The congruence means x is an exact multiple of 2^k.

passages.title: XOR identifies a sibling under these assumptions
passages.text: The two children of a size-2^(k+1) interval differ in exactly bit k. Thus the buddy offset of x is x xor 2ᵏ. For a nonzero arena base B, compute B+((address−B) xor 2ᵏ), not blindly absolute-address XOR unless the alignment makes that equivalent. A buddy must be within this arena, free, and have the same current order. XOR compares binary digits and flips a digit exactly where one input has 1 and the other 0. XOR with 2^k flips only bit k, exchanging the two equal halves of one parent block.

passages.title: Merge only the two halves of one parent
passages.text: Two adjacent eight-byte blocks at offsets 8 and 16 are not buddies: their buddies are 0 and 24. Every stage remains a disjoint partition of the original arena.

passages.title: Measure rounding waste and failure
passages.text: A request just above a power of two can reserve almost twice its payload, even with no external holes. That is internal rounding waste. The implementation stores bookkeeping out of band in this abstract model; a real allocator must account for its own metadata and minimum order. An exact-power request does not round further. If no suitable block exists, report failure without modifying any free set or live allocation.

title: Compare allocation under a workload

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Measure fragmentation, search work and utilization; scrutinize probabilistic assumptions. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

passages.title: An experiment needs a specified workload
passages.text: Compare policies on the identical ordered sequence of allocations and releases, with the same arena, alignment, overhead and tie-breaking. Our first experiment is a fully listed deterministic trace, not a sample from an unnamed random distribution. We measure success, free-list probes, payload utilization, reserved bytes and hole sizes. Different policies may start diverging after the same release because their earlier placement decisions differed. U is payload utilization and C the full arena capacity in bytes. Reserved padding does not count as live payload in its numerator.

passages.title: Keep failure semantics identical
passages.text: If a named allocation fails, a later release of that name must be handled consistently; otherwise one policy receives an invalid workload and the comparison becomes meaningless. The shown trace is chosen to make all its releases valid. First fit counts each inspected free-list entry until success; best fit counts the entire candidate scan. Both models coalesce on release and split with the same minimum remainder.

passages.title: A smaller immediate hole can hurt later
passages.text: In the trace, first fit places a ten-byte request into an earlier twenty-byte hole, whereas best fit can choose a twelve-byte hole. Those locally reasonable choices leave different possibilities for the next eighteen-byte request. The scene aligns both address lanes and updates measured probe counts from the executed search. No conclusion is inferred from the names “best” and “first.”

title: Use a known size distribution carefully

sections.title: Use a known size distribution carefully

passages.title: A forecast can determine an inventory
passages.text: Distributed fit pre-partitions storage into fixed slots of different capacities, at most one allocation per slot. Slots are sorted by size, making first adequate empty and smallest adequate empty equivalent searches under the same tie order. The source’s scheme assumes a known size distribution and that every present block is equally likely to depart next, independently of its age. These are consequential workload hypotheses, not implementation details. N_live counts allocations currently present, and v names one of them. The probability formula gives every such allocation the same chance to be the next departure.

passages.title: Do not turn an asymptotic reserve into a guarantee
passages.text: The source discusses roughly N primary slots matched to the size distribution plus √N log₂N maximum-sized overflow slots. Under its probabilistic model this yields reserve overhead of order N^(−1/2) log N relative to primary storage as N grows. A finite instance still pays actual bytes, and mismatched sizes or lifetimes void the inference. Our small deterministic inventory illustrates that risk; it is not a simulation proving the asymptotic theorem.

title: Handle overflow without corrupting live data

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original prose, examples, diagrams and assessments. Source formulas and algorithm conditions checked against the supplied edition; no textbook pages, exercise text or scans are included.
scope: Selective companion treatment: Distinguish exhaustion from fragmentation; reason about compaction, relocation and graceful failure. Exact finite models supplement, rather than replace, the mathematical arguments.

sections.title: Handle overflow without corrupting live data

passages.title: Classify a failed request before recovering
passages.text: Failure may mean aggregate exhaustion, external fragmentation, an alignment or metadata constraint, or arithmetic overflow while computing a size. The arena here has two separated holes totaling half its capacity; a half-capacity request still cannot fit. Rejecting it is correct. Failure must have an explicit result and leave the previous live allocations valid.

passages.title: Validate arithmetic before any mutation
passages.text: For an unsigned w-bit size type, ensure payload plus metadata plus alignment slack does not exceed 2ʷ−1 before adding. Check every computed endpoint against arena bounds. Only after all checks and a suitable free block are found should the allocator commit list and tag changes. Python integers do not overflow; our bounded-size guard deliberately models this implementation obligation instead of relying on Python’s unlimited arithmetic. In the guard, r is payload size, h metadata overhead, a alignment, and MAX=2^w−1 the largest representable unsigned size. Subtracting the overhead and worst-case padding before testing r avoids overflowing the addition itself.

passages.title: A failed search is a no-op, a later release is not
passages.text: The model snapshots every block, attempts the impossible allocation, and verifies exact equality afterward. It then releases the live block between the holes, coalesces, and retries successfully. The successful retry is caused by a legitimate change in storage state, not by weakening the allocation contract. Search counters may change on failure, but allocation metadata and live payloads do not.

passages.title: Moving objects requires moving all references
passages.text: Compaction can combine nonadjacent holes only by relocating live blocks. Every root and interior pointer must then be updated, or references must use stable handles that are redirected consistently. Unknown raw pointers, pinned objects, and external references can prevent compaction. Reclaiming unreachable objects or spilling data also needs its own correctness contract. No recovery strategy creates capacity when all bytes are genuinely required.

title: Pointer machines connect the whole chapter

sections.title: Pointer machines connect the whole chapter

passages.title: Describe the abstract machine before counting steps
passages.text: A pointer machine has a fixed number of pointer registers, nodes with a fixed number of link and information fields, and instructions such as create, copy a pointer, test equality, read or write a field of a held node, and follow a link. Null is a distinguished non-object value. Only objects currently held in registers are immediately accessible; the machine cannot name an arbitrary distant object by arithmetic unless the model explicitly adds that operation. V is the set of allocated object identities; null is an extra marker outside that set. Membership in V∪{null} specifies what a pointer register may hold.

passages.title: Representation invariants connect the chapter
passages.text: Tree parent links, same-name indexes, allocation handles and garbage-collection roots are all constrained uses of this linked-node state. A traversal proof specifies which links may be followed; a collector proof specifies which identities remain live; an allocator proof specifies where their finite bytes reside. Changing one representation requires rechecking the algorithms that depend on its invariants. This synthesis is instructional material from the end of the historical section, not an interactive bibliography.

passages.title: Abstract constant time is a modeling assumption
passages.text: Treating one pointer operation as unit cost ignores finite address width, cache locality, allocation failure and physical memory limits. A w-bit address field can encode only finitely many locations, so an unbounded-node abstract machine is not a literal finite implementation. Graph-local rewriting machines use a different access rule; this unit does not assert unrestricted constant-factor equivalence. Choose the model whose operations match the question being analyzed.
